Tell me about Novo Nordisk

source: Tom's own account

Novo Nordisk is a global pharmaceutical company, best known for its treatments in obesity and diabetes. I worked at Novo for almost 6 years (2020 to 2026).

I joined Novo as a Senior Product Manager, to build a digital patient solution for Wegovy, a then-unheard-of weight loss medicine. I led the full product lifecycle end to end, and it was really a stealth transformation project, where I could bring my learnings from LEO but to in-house transformation.

I was later asked to scale learnings from Wegovycare across the product organisation and was promoted to Associate Product Director. In this role, I had a much wider remit, and worked on high-impact, cross-functional projects across the organisation.

Want to know more? Ask about either of my roles, the transformation work, or specific projects like Wegovy or the GenAI proof of concept.

Tell me about the Wegovycare role

source: Tom's own account

Senior Product Manager at Novo Nordisk (Mar 2020 - Feb 2022), building Wegovycare - a retention-focused digital service to increase repeat prescriptions for Wegovy.

I led the full product lifecycle end to end, but it was really a stealth transformation project, where I could bring my learnings from LEO but this time to in-house transformation.

Key achievements:

  • Led the full product life-cycle, introducing discovery, rapid prototyping, iterative development, and automated documentation to the organisation.
  • Automated documentation and shifted release cycles from yearly to bi-monthly in high-regulation environment, enabling iterative learning.
  • Built a weight-loss prediction algorithm from concept to prototype (later spun out into a new API product)
  • Achieved 10% penetration in our first national market

I was asked to scale these learnings across the product organisation and was promoted to Associate Product Director.

How did you change ways of working at Novo?

source: Tom's own account

Innovation Labs are an interesting idea, but unfortunately rarely work in practice. I still believed there was enormous potential in healthcare, so this time wanted to try it from the inside - transformation by doing.

I got my first opportunity in my final round job interview at Novo, when I convinced the business to set-aside their solution-first brief, and to talk to patients and start with the problem instead. I was fortunate enough to be offered the role, and use this as a mandate to completely reinvent their ways of working. We were the first product team to interview patients, run discovery, make prototypes, co-create with markets and so on. It wasn't straight-forward and took persuasion and a leap of faith from our stakeholders, but the results spoke for themselves.

I was asked to scale these learnings across the product organisation and was promoted to Associate Product Director.

Tell me about a GenAI project

source: Tom's own account

When developing health software, every release needs extensive regulatory review by medical, legal and regulatory experts (pharma calls it MLR). The process was designed for simple marketing materials, not sophisticated software - but it hadn't evolved.

In practice, every screen had to be captured in PDF format and reviewed individually. The result: significant delays (backlogs could mean months), huge documentation overhead, and an anti-pattern where you had to fully develop everything before getting sign-off.

I used an internal LLM sandbox to create a RAG model that captured the various guidelines and regulations. Now we could automatically document and review each submission with a full audit trail - the review team only had to rubber-stamp the release.

I also built a prototype agent that plugged into Figma, so designers could query the guidelines before investing too much effort. This allowed product teams to shift left - fail in design, not at review.

The product teams loved it. Organisational priorities later shifted and the project was handed to another team, but the proof of concept showed a clear path to dramatically faster release cycles.
